A content delivery network is a system of computers spread across many cities that store copies of websites so people can load pages faster. Normally, every request travels to one origin server, the single main computer where a website's files originally live. If that computer sits far away, pages load slowly, and heavy traffic can overwhelm it. A content delivery network solves this by placing copies of the content on servers closer to visitors, called edge locations, since they sit at the edge of the network, nearer to homes and offices than the origin server. When a request arrives, the network checks whether the nearby edge location already has a saved copy. If it does, that is called a cache hit, and the page appears almost instantly without contacting the origin server at all. If not, the edge location fetches the content once, stores it, and serves it quickly to everyone afterward. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries holding copies of popular books, so borrowers do not need to travel across the country to the one library that owns the original copy. This setup reduces waiting time, spreads out traffic so no single computer gets overloaded, and keeps websites working even during sudden surges of visitors. The result is a smoother, more reliable experience for anyone browsing online, whether reading news, watching videos, or shopping.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|------|----------------|-----------------|
| Origin server | The original computer storing a website's files | It is the source everyone ultimately depends on |
| Edge location | A nearby server holding copies of content | It shortens travel distance for faster loading |
| Cache hit | A successful request answered by a saved copy | It avoids delay from reaching the origin server |
| Content delivery network | The whole network of edge locations working together | It keeps websites fast and stable under heavy demand |
